tedious

/TEE-dee-uhs/ - the stress falls on TEE · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tedious means dull and boringly repetitive.

The customs form was only two pages; the tedious part was copying the same serial numbers onto six carbon copies.

Worked Example

The lighthouse logbook demanded an entry every hour: wind, visibility, lamp status. Wind, visibility, lamp status. Keeper after keeper filled decades of pages with weather that refused to change, and more than one journal ends mid-sentence, as if the pen itself had yawned. The sea was dangerous nine nights a year; the other three hundred and fifty-six were merely tedious.

Tedious is the exact word because it needs the drag of repetition: dull, and dull again, and dull in exactly the same way for hours. A bad lecture can be boring for twenty minutes; tedium is boredom with a schedule. If the task were varied or the pages surprising, plainer words would do — tedious promises that tomorrow's entry will match today's.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tiresome: Tiresome things wear your patience — a squeaky door, a friend's third retelling of the same story. Tedious adds the drag of repetition stretched over real time: the hundredth identical entry, hour after hour. A single interruption can be tiresome; tedious needs the long haul of sameness.

humdrum: Humdrum is the flavor of everyday, eventless routine — the commute, the weekly shop, the same sandwich at the same desk. Tedious is sharper: the sameness has begun to ache. A humdrum week just passes without incident; a tedious afternoon grinds while you watch every minute of it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

gripping: holds attention hard

fascinating: draws you in and keeps you asking

Where it sits · how hard the sameness wears you down — dull → tedious → mind-numbing

dull vs. tedious: A dull afternoon just fails to interest; a tedious one grinds — the same dull minute, replayed until it aches.

mind-numbing vs. tedious: Mind-numbing goes past tedious: tedious work makes you watch the clock, while mind-numbing work makes you forget the clock exists — attention doesn't drift, it shuts down.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tedi

Root — tedi: weariness

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Tedi (weariness, from Latin taedium) + -ous (full of) = full of weariness. Latin taedet meant 'it wearies' — a verb for the special exhaustion of sameness. English took the noun too, as tedium, so the word carries its own name for what it inflicts.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin taedium built only its own small household in English — tedious and its noun, tedium — and nothing farther afield. There is no far-off cousin to discover; the family album is two faces, both yawning.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / weary

Tedious is for the long haul of sameness — forms, drills, inventories — dullness stretched over time by repetition. It judges the task, not you: plenty of tedious work is vital work. Note where it stops: an exhausting day may be thrilling, and a tedious one may cost no sweat at all; the word measures boredom, never effort.
